description: Team Red-Shift — we look at the universe a little differently. We’re a team driven by curiosity for what’s beyond Earth and the technology needed to understand it. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we’re diving into Planet X and SPHEREx, exploring the mission’s infrared observations and the stories hidden within vast amounts of cosmic data. We build, question, experiment, and keep pushing until the idea becomes real.

details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPHEREx Explorer (Project Red-Shift) is a web platform that makes SPHEREx spectral data easy to explore and compare. SPHEREx observes the sky in 102 infrared spectral bands, but its raw spectral images are hard for non-specialists to work with. Our platform turns them into measured spectra that researchers, students, and the public can browse and compare in a modern interface.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline using astropy and photutils processes SPHEREx Quick Release 2 spectral images from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). It detects 72 sources and measures each one in every exposure, producing 8,640 spectrum points. Gaia DR3 serves as the reference catalogue, and literature links point to NASA ADS. We also added featured stars (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi, WISE 0855-0714, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis) so users can look at well-known objects of different types and check them against published references. For moving-object screening, we compared a second epoch from the IRSA collection spherex_dr1_deep. This supports the Planet X side of the challenge by flagging candidate moving sources.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

We want vital space science to reach a wider audience. Users can go from raw data to meaningful insight without writing code, so students can learn from real observations and researchers can quickly inspect and compare sources.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE AND TRUSTWORTHY

We designed the platform around data honesty:

- Missing data stays empty. It is never filled in or interpolated.

- Points that may be affected by flagged pixels or image edges are marked "suspect" and kept visible, not hidden.

- Candidates from the two-epoch screening are presented as candidates only and need independent confirmation.

Showing uncertainty openly, instead of a polished but misleading result, was a deliberate choice.

TOOLS AND AI USE

Python (astropy, photutils) for the data pipeline, and a web application deployed at spherex-and-planetx.vercel.app. We used Google AI Studio and Google Stitch to generate and design the app, Claude for planning and code review, and CapCut for video subtitles (auto-generated and proofread by the team). All numbers come from tested Python code, and every result was checked against the real data and IRSA documentation.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Data quality (flagged pixels and image edges), reproducibility from public archives (IRSA, Gaia DR3, DOI 10.26131/IRSA652), accessibility for non-experts, and being clear about the limits of what the data can show.

Code: https://github.com/Ashhajj0/SPHEREX-And-PLANETX

Live app: https://spherex-and-planetx.vercel.app/
